items.title: OpenAI reportedly raises $11B at a $1.25T valuation
items.summary: OpenAI has reportedly raised an additional $11 billion in a new funding round that values the company at $1.25 trillion, according to Bloomberg. The $11 billion is part of a larger round that has not closed and could total about $20 billion; The Verge notes OpenAI previously raised $122 billion in March at an $852 billion valuation and had hoped for as much as $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation.
items.comment: The reported raise falls short of earlier targets, so the valuation gap may be worth watching.

items.title: Crusoe sells unfinished Wyoming data center project to Google
items.summary: Crusoe confirmed it sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google, which announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the campus. Crusoe had initially announced the project with Tallgrass and planned to scale it to 10 gigawatts; Google did not disclose how much it paid. Crusoe is still developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.
items.comment: The handoff may underscore execution risk in very large AI campuses.

items.title: Meta pauses business terms update that would allow AI training on linked sites
items.summary: Meta has indefinitely delayed a commercial terms update that would have required Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook. The company said existing terms remain in effect; the changes had been pushed from October 30 to November 20 after courts in Brazil and Norway issued preliminary injunctions and the UK's competition authority opened an investigation.
items.comment: The pause may ease immediate publisher pressure, but the underlying dispute over AI training data is unresolved.

items.title: US midterms spark AI stock selloff and fresh datacenter moratorium calls
items.summary: After Democrats' midterm victories, the Nasdaq had its worst day in 19 months on Thursday, falling 5.5%, and European and Asian markets fell on Friday. TechCrunch reported that the public voted on 41 data center-related ballot measures on Tuesday and, in all but one, the majority voted to impose more restrictions. Senator Bernie Sanders and several newly elected Democrats renewed calls for datacenter moratoriums.
items.comment: The market reaction may reflect valuation anxiety as much as election results, but policy pressure looks real.

items.title: METR report finds Anthropic's AI research speed roughly doubled
items.summary: A METR report following an 11-week investigation inside Anthropic found the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, amounting to roughly two years of historical progress over the last year. METR said it was confident the acceleration was not simply due to scaling compute, with the majority due to AI; Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the report.
items.comment: The redactions may make it hard for outsiders to judge the full evidence behind the finding.

items.title: US approved Nvidia H200 sales to China-linked firm with an empty office, NYT reports
items.summary: The New York Times reported that New Matrix is on the list of approved firms to handle Nvidia's H200 AI chips, but its offices were empty and there was little evidence the company exists in a meaningful way. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm blacklisted by the US since 2024, and concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing due diligence. The Trump administration relaxed restrictions after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15% cut of sales.
items.comment: The report may invite more congressional scrutiny of export controls.

items.title: China reportedly recruited Megaspeed executive to spy on Nvidia's Jensen Huang
items.summary: The New York Times reported that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The report says she was enlisted to glean information about American AI chips and potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China. Three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang.
items.comment: The reported briefing request suggests congressional scrutiny may intensify.

items.title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tool deployments found exposed online
items.summary: Censys said it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex, an open-source autonomous penetration testing tool, that were accessible from the web without a password. Artex has been linked to cyberattacks including against the Korean finance industry in September and IT support giant ConnectWise in October. Microsoft has described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little human interaction.
items.comment: Misconfigured deployments may become a ready supply of attack infrastructure.

items.title: Open-weight Chinese models near closed frontier models in hacking tests
items.summary: Vals tested AI models on mock corporate networks and found OpenAI's trusted-access cyber model Daybreak completed 81% of tasks on average, while the Chinese open-weight model DeepSeek completed 73%. On some tasks the two models scored equally, and Vals estimated an attack cost $17 to $46 in tokens for GPT-6-Sol versus $2 to $3 for DeepSeek. The findings suggest closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills.
items.comment: The findings may intensify debate over gated access to cyber-capable models.

items.title: Three men charged with using AI to impersonate executives and steal over $129M
items.summary: The US Department of Justice unsealed an indictment charging Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit with using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys to convince employees to send large payments. The men allegedly stole more than $129 million from companies worldwide between 2024 and 2026; Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain and Sheetrit in the United Kingdom.
items.comment: The case may test how existing fraud law handles AI-generated impersonation.

items.title: DataVita's Lanarkshire AI datacenter to be fully grid-served, not directly renewable
items.summary: DataVita has revised its plan for the Chapelhall AI development near Glasgow, saying the datacenters will be fully served by the National Grid with the possibility that solar and wind farms could connect in the future. It had promised the project would draw 1GW from green sources, and it still receives £202 million in wealth guarantees from the UK's national wealth fund. The project was a key plank of the UK's AI strategy, with plans for a 500MW datacenter and 3,400 jobs.
items.comment: The revision may complicate the UK's AI growth zone claims.

items.title: South-east Asia's datacenter buildout hits power and water constraints
items.summary: Thailand paused construction on 49 datacenter projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, while the governor of Indonesia's West Java province halted a datacenter over missing permits and an incomplete environmental assessment. South-east Asia has the largest share of under-construction datacenter capacity in Asia Pacific, about 50%, according to Cushman and Wakefield. Malaysia's Johor state grew operational capacity from 94MW in 2023 to 1,110MW in 2026.
items.comment: Power and water constraints may slow the region's data center growth more than demand does.

items.title: Activists storm Microsoft datacenter site in Amsterdam amid Europe-wide protests
items.summary: Activists from the Dutch group Geef Tegengas broke into a Microsoft datacenter construction site in Westpoort, Amsterdam, clashing with police; some climbed a crane, lit flares, and tied helium balloons to equipment. The action came amid a Europe-wide 'Stop Dirty Data Centres' campaign with protests in Bristol, Berlin, Warsaw, and Zagreb demanding moratoria on new datacenters. Police said an officer was slightly injured.
items.comment: The protests signal that datacenter opposition is spreading beyond the US.

items.title: AI labs' appetite for work files and emails fuels data-acquisition market
items.summary: WIRED received pitches offering $350,000 to $1.8 million, and in one case up to $2 million, for old work records such as documents, emails, Slack messages, tickets, and call transcripts for AI training. Handshake confirmed it licenses professional documents across fields including journalism and said a big part of its business is buying graduate students' papers and coursework. Anthropic said it does not buy workflow from live companies like WIRED, while OpenAI did not respond before publication.
items.comment: The market's scale is difficult to verify, but the pitches show demand for private workflow data.

items.title: Meta launches Spaces for its Muse AI agent
items.summary: Meta launched Spaces, custom app-like experiences inside its Muse agent that users create by describing a tracker, planner, or project board; Spaces can connect third-party apps and update in the background. Meta is rolling the feature out to all Muse users and is also bringing Active Memory and Active Focus capabilities from its Muse Wonder model into the app. Zuckerberg said in October that Muse agents had 10 million users in the US and Canada.
items.comment: The feature may test whether agentic assistants can move beyond chat into everyday organization.

items.title: NYT Cooking tests AI assistant for recipe modifications
items.summary: NYT Cooking is testing an AI assistant, available to subscribers on iOS only at launch, that suggests recipe modifications and was trained on user comments. The Verge reviewer tested it on ingredient swaps, recipe scaling, and a missing Bundt pan.
items.comment: The review suggests narrow, comment-informed assistance may land better than fully AI-generated recipes.

items.title: AI-assisted reverse engineering could pressure Rockstar on GTA VI PC port
items.summary: Former Rockstar tech director Obbe Vermeij told Rock Paper Shotgun he would be concerned that someone could use AI to convert the PS5 version of GTA VI to PC. He speculated that reverse-engineering could cost tens of thousands of dollars in tokens and that the resulting port probably would not match Rockstar's effort but might satisfy some PC players. Ars Technica notes that AI-powered reverse-engineering tools can quickly turn console game binaries into easy-to-port code.
items.comment: The timing threat is speculative, but it shows how AI coding tools may unsettle game platform strategy.

items.title: Every Mac since macOS 13 builds an undocumented personal knowledge graph for Apple Intelligence
items.summary: A technical analysis says every Mac since macOS 13 ships daemons that build a graph of who you know, relationships, communications, locations, and activities by cross-referencing Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, and Screen Time. The post says the graph is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from, and it publishes a tool to inspect the graph.
items.comment: Technical practice; the LLM-retrieval claim is the author's analysis and may warrant independent verification.
